entries.value: I save old buildings; not people.
2003 was an accident. I didn’t change Tomás’s report; whoever changed it changed it.

I took the tiles out before the fire, yes; Julián didn’t know. For twenty-seven years I’ve used a few in every restoration as ‘original’, the foundation’s adviser approves, the money comes. Esperanza saw them at the Alcázar. ‘Tomorrow I’m going to bube,’ she said. The mould was right by my hand. I threw it in the barrel, I lit the kiln. I didn’t know about the sensor.
You struck Esperanza with the mould.
I went, about an order. I left at half past ten. Esperanza was fine, old, forgetful. She must have lit the kiln at night and fallen asleep; Julián did the same in 2003.
He pulls out the end of his tape measure and lets it snap back.
Did you go to the workshop last night?

A file reopened from the archive (4 June 2003, closed as an ‘accident’):

· Workshop fire; the master Julián Vidal (51) died in the kiln room.
· First report of the assessor Tomás Herrera (removed from the file, in the archive’s back pocket): traces of accelerant, door bolted from the outside.
· Witness on the night of the fire: the workshop’s tile carrier at the time, Álvaro Méndez — ‘the kiln was faulty, Julián knew it.’
· ‘Burnt’ stock: 340 hand-painted 18th-century reproductions; insured value €410,000.
The fire closed as an ‘accident’ twenty-seven years ago has been reopened.

· No soot in the airways, low carbon monoxide in the blood: the victim was dead before the smoke spread.
· Cause of death: a single blow to the back left of the head with a heavy, angular object. White plaster dust in the wound.
· Time of death: 23.00–00.30. The kiln was started at 01.10.
The master dies from a single blow to the back of the head.
The master calls her daughter: ‘The fire didn’t kill your father.’
The kiln is started by hand.
The apprentice leaves the workshop; the contractor is coming.
Where did the plaster mould go?
To the bottom of the workshop’s clay barrel
The mould wasn’t in the kiln.
It was recorded that the pieces of the mould were found at the bottom of the clay barrel.
There were tiles in the van, but no mould.
The death was ruled a kiln accident; the workshop was sold.
Álvaro Méndez was arrested; the 2003 fire was reopened as ‘deliberate’. The Fundación Santa Ana restoration approvals signed ‘E. V.’ went into the Triana branch’s file.
Nuria Vidal was taken into custody; the restoration went on.
Rocío Navarro was arrested; the 2003 file stayed in the archive.
The victim died from a blow to the head before the smoke spread; the kiln was lit by hand after her death.

The thumbprint on the kiln dial is his, his boots carry the barrel’s clay; the tiles ‘burnt’ in 2003 came out of his van. The reopened 2003 file shows why the victim was going to bube and why he stopped her.
The daughter was in Madrid that night; she told of her mother’s last words.
The apprentice left at nine; the print on the dial isn’t hers.
She fell and hit her head
She was struck on the head with a plaster mould; the kiln was lit afterwards

She called last night at eight, the first time in a year. ‘Nuria, the fire didn’t kill your father,’ she said. ‘Álvaro was here that night. The insurance man knew too.’ I… I said, ‘Mum, again?’ I hung up. She’d been saying it for twenty-seven years.
She tightens the belt of her trench coat.
When did you last speak to your mother?
I hadn’t spoken to my mother for a year.
In Triana a master tile-maker was found dead in her kiln room. In 2003 the same workshop burnt down.
45, the victim’s daughter; lives in Madrid.
69, retired insurance assessor; he examined the 2003 fire.

On the morning of 17 October 2030, in Triana, the master Esperanza Vidal (74) was found dead in the kiln room of a tile workshop on Calle Alfarería. The kiln had run during the night and been shut off by the safety sensor; the room was full of smoke.

Her apprentice Rocío Navarro found the body at 08.00. The victim’s daughter Nuria Vidal set off from Madrid. The workshop’s biggest customer is the restoration contractor Álvaro Méndez.
Request permission to open the 2003 fire file from the archive
Request permission to search Álvaro Méndez’s van
Request a crime scene examination of the workshop

Nobody. The master never lit the kiln at night, never after 2003. After that fire she had the safety sensor fitted herself. In the morning the clay in the barrel was strange too, as if it had been stirred; I’d left it to rest in the evening.
Who runs the kiln at night?

At nine. The master said, ‘Álvaro’s coming, we’ll talk, you go.’ She was tense. Last week at the restoration in the Alcázar she’d seen our tiles; ‘those burnt in 2003, Rocío, I swept up their ashes with my own eyes,’ she said.
She wipes the clay off her cheek with the back of her hand.
When did you leave the workshop last night?

The apprentice told of the master’s suspicion, the daughter of the last phone call, the assessor of the removed report; those got the 2003 file opened. The autopsy showed death came before the smoke, the workshop examination gave the mould and the print. The search found the ‘burnt’ tiles.
The sensor that put out a fire was fitted by the wife of the man who died in the first one.

In 2003 the carrier Álvaro Méndez took 340 of the Vidal workshop’s tiles out before the fire and set the kiln room alight with the door bolted from outside; Julián Vidal died, the insurance paid out, the assessor’s report was removed from the file. Twenty-seven years later the master Esperanza saw those tiles in a restoration. Álvaro struck her with a plaster mould, threw the mould into the clay barrel and lit the kiln; the sensor she had fitted after 2003 shut the kiln off.

I wrote my report: traces of accelerant beside the kiln, door bolted from outside. ‘Suspicious fire,’ I said. The company paid, the file closed as an ‘accident’; another report was put in place of mine. The value of the stock recorded as destroyed in the fire was almost the insured sum. Nobody asked back then who had carried that stock.
He pushes his glasses up his nose.

Álvaro Méndez’s van and storeroom (with the branch chief’s approval):

· Twelve hand-painted tiles wrapped in newspaper; on the back, Julián Vidal’s pre-2003 workshop stamp. They are on the ‘burnt stock’ list in the 2003 file.
· On the van’s pedal and on Álvaro Méndez’s boots, the same clay as in the tile workshop’s clay barrel; the thumbprint on the kiln dial is his.
· Fundación Santa Ana restoration approval forms: ‘original, 18th century’; adviser’s signature ‘E. V.’.

· The kiln programme was started by hand at 01.10; on the dial, a clay-dusted thumbprint — not the master’s or the apprentice’s.
· At the bottom of the clay barrel, a broken plaster mould; on its corner, the victim’s blood and hair.
· The kiln room door was not bolted from inside; a fresh scuff mark on the outer bolt.
Broken pieces of plaster mould from the bottom of the clay barrel; dried blood on one.
Twelve tiles from a van, recorded as destroyed in the 2003 fire.
The kiln’s digital panel; the programme was started by hand at 01.10 at night.
